title: Throwing a Ball on the Moon
learningObjectives: Explain that a Moon throw has no drag and follows ballistic flight with only weight acting.
Describe horizontal speed staying constant while vertical speed falls at rate g.
Use the highest-point relation to compare how high the same throw rises on the Moon versus Earth.

sources.title: Throwing a ball on the Moon (project-authored test text)
sources.attribution: Written by the Make knowledge interactive project team for testing.

evidence.quote: On the Moon there is no air, so a thrown ball feels no drag at all.

explanations.text: A thrown ball on the Moon feels no air drag, so its flight is purely ballistic with only weight pulling straight down.

evidence.quote: Nothing pushes the ball sideways, so the horizontal speed stays U0 for the whole flight
Vertically, gravity slows the ball at a steady rate g.

explanations.text: With no sideways push the horizontal speed stays constant while gravity slows vertical motion at steady rate g.

evidence.quote: The ball stops rising when V = 0, which happens at t = V0 / g.
Because g on the Moon is about six times smaller, the same throw rises about six times higher than on Earth.

explanations.text: The ball stops rising when vertical speed reaches zero, so maximum height grows when gravity is smaller, as on the Moon.

predictions.prompt: Throw a ball on the Moon with no air drag where g is about 1.62 m/s^2, using horizontal speed 10 m/s and vertical speed 8 m/s. Predict the maximum height.
Throw the same ball with horizontal speed 10 m/s and vertical speed 8 m/s on Earth where g is 9.8 m/s^2. Predict the maximum height.
Throw a ball higher on the Moon where g is about 1.62 m/s^2 with horizontal speed 12 m/s and vertical speed 12 m/s. Predict the maximum height.
